VAN ZANDT COUNTY.
One Negro Killed and Three Mortally Wounded—Causes of the Affray.
Special Telegram to the Statesman.

CANTON, November 2.—Jim Bell was killed and Ben Russell and George Washington and Tom Griffin were mortally wounded Wednesday night. A capias had been issued for the arrest of Russell for disturbing the peace. Four white men, W. L. Hays, Sam Stanford, Claud Stanford and Will James, went to make the arrest. Bell and Griffin were with Russell. The three men were called upon to hold up their hands, but before they could comply they were fired upon with the result as above. All the men shot are colored. It is claimed that the white men tried to get Russell to join the union labor party, but Russell said he would vote the democratic ticket. The officers are trying to find the white men who went to arrest Russell.

Bradstreet's will say to-day in its review of the state of trade: "Our special telegrams this week furnish evidence of increased confidence East and West as to the prospect for the autumn's trade. Mercantile collections are irregular, being fairly satisfactory at Pittsburgh, Chicago, St. Louis and Burlington, but disappointing at Kansas City, St. Joseph, St. Paul and Detroit. Terrific Storm at Jamestown.

XENIA, O., Aug. 18.—The storm Thursday afternoon was terrific at Jamestown, when the fair was in progress. NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 20.—Dr. W. F. Simmons, an ex-member of the legislature, was shot twice in his store, twelve miles east of Osyke, Miss., Saturday by Lee Hinson. His wounds are pronounced fatal. Simmons had taken a very decided stand against the practice of "regulating," and thus incurred the enmity of Hinson and others.

A murder and lynching in McDowell County, W. Va., is reported. The parties concerned were Mr. and Mrs. Milt Hawks, Charles Duncan, a young man, and an indignant populace, in a locality off the lines of railroad. Mr. and Mrs. Hawks quarreled; Duncan, who was living with them, interfered, taking Mrs. Hawks' part. Hawks then attacked Duncan, who drew a revolver and shot Hawks through the heart, killing him instantly. Duncan fled, hiding himself for two days in a bed, where an indignant mob found him, some miles from where the shooting occurred. He was taken before a justice and given a preliminary examination, when his own prevarications proved his guilt, and he was sent to jail. While on his way a mob followed him, and, taking him from the officers, lynched him by hanging him to a tree. There will probably be nothing done in the matter, as all the parties bore bad reputations.

PARKERSBURG, March 5.—In Harrisonville, in McDowell county, Mr. and Mrs. Mitil Hawks quarreled, and Duncan, a young man boarding with them, took the part of Mrs. Hawks. This enraged Hawks, who began abusing Duncan, saying he interfered too often in favor of his wife. The altercation resulted in Duncan shooting Hawks through the heart. Duncan escaped, and remained hid for two days, when he was found by a mob. He was taken before a justice and a preliminary trial held. The testimony of the woman, and of Duncan, was such that the justice sent Duncan to jail. The mob awaited the result of the trial, and while Duncan was being taken to jail, overpowered the officers and took him away. No resistance to their action was made, and they took him to the woods and hanged him to a tree

Mysteriously Shot While Running with a Crowd at His Heels.

MACON, GA., Sept. 4.—Ernest Williams, a negro thief and desperado, was shot and instantly killed this afternoon while attempting to escape arrest. The exact particulars of the affair are hard to get. Williams, who was a professional thief, and who, besides having served several terms in the chain-gang and penitentiary, had given the officers much trouble, became engaged in a row in the early part of the afternoon in a Fourth street dive. Officer Murphy attempted to arrest Williams, but he ran. He was pursued to the corner of Third and Elm streets by an excited crowd, when several shots were indiscriminately fired at him.

KILLED ALMOST INSTANTLY.

He fell shot through the back and died almost instantly, the ball having passed entirely through his body. There are conflicting statements as to who did the shooting. It is almost certain that it was not done by the officers. A brother-in-law of the dead negro positively asserted that he was shot by a negro in the pursuing crowd, who had been an enemy of Williams. He was a bad negro and was feared by every one. His field of action extended over several counties. Before any particulars could be obtained Samuel Battle and William Williams (colored), attempted to incite the crowd of excited negroes who had gathered to riot, but by prompt action further violence was averted. Eight shots were fired in all. The coroner empanneled a jury. An examination was made of the body, when the inquest was adjourned until to-morrow noon.

Daniel Lucas Apt to be Held for the Killing of Williams.
Daniel Lucas Apt to be Held for the Killing of Williams.

MACON, GA., Sept. 5.—The excitement over the Ernest Williams case still continues. At the coroner's inquest to-day three witnesses—James Pope, Henry Collins and Robert Colburn (all colored)—testified positively that Daniel Lucas, a white man, fired the shot that killed Williams. All agreed that Lucas was behind Officer Johnson, who had fired one shot in the air to frighten Williams, when Lucas ran about 10 feet in front of the officer and leveled his pistol at Williams. Williams then staggered and fell. Lucas was within 30 feet of Williams when he fired. A post mortem examination revealed that Williams had been shot through the liver. No verdict has yet been returned, but it is probable that Lucas will be held.

Mysterious Disappearance of Two Mormon Elders in Alabama.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., August 23.—[Special.]

News comes from Clay county, in the eastern part of the state, of the mysterious disappearance and supposed murder of two Mormon elders, Davis and Weaver, who have been preaching in that section for some time.

Mormon missionaries have been working in Clay county for about four years and have made many converts. They established a flourishing mission station and have met with little opposition until quite recently. Most of the converts made have been women and they were hurried off to Utah.

A short time ago, one of these converts wrote a letter from Salt Lake City to relatives in Clay county. The letter told a terrible story of the horrors of a life of polygamy and the outrages to which the writer and other Alabama converts had been subjected.

This aroused the people of Clay county, and the Mormon elders were ordered to leave, but they refused to obey the order. The feeling against them among the better class of citizens was stirred to fever heat last Sunday, by a baptising conducted by Elders Davis and Weaver. It is said that these elders took several converts of both sexes to a mill pond and taking them into the water in a perfectly nude condition immersed them in the presence of about fifty people.

When this became known throughout the neighborhood many threats against the Mormon elders were made. Monday night a body of masked men went to the house where Elders Davis and Weaver were boarding and ordered them to leave the county within twenty-four hours. It is said the elders defied the crowd, and the next morning started alone for the neighborhood of Lineville to hold services at the house of a convert, and since that time they have not been seen or heard of, but it is generally believed they have been murdered and their bodies concealed by the indignant citizens of the county.

We learn from Mr. Brede, after our first account of the shooting had been printed, that after Adams was shot by Hoppe he sprang from under the wagon where he was laying and endeavored to take the pistol away from the murderer, and that quite a scuffle followed between the two men. Adams finding that he was growing weak from the loss of blood, and that he could not hold out much longer said "I see Gus (Mr. Brede) coming!" With that the murderer let go Adams and ran to the wagon and seized the rifle and left. This accounts for the blood on Hoppe's shirt. Mr. Scott says it was proposed by some to arrest the fellow immediately and hold him, but others objected to acting too hastily, for fear of getting themselves into trouble. He left before any definite action had been taken and does not know whether the miners concluded to put Hoppe under arrest or not.

Mr. Scott reached Conrad Friday afternoon and there met Deputy Sheriff Crawford and told him where Hoppe was. Mr. Crawford took a fresh team and started immediately for the Sweet Grass mines, where it is likely he will catch Hoppe, who probably remained in the Hills all day and the night of Friday, as he was about worn out with fatigue and did not seem to be in any hurry to get away. Deputy Crawford would reach the mines sometime during the night, and unless Hoppe had taken to the hills and secreted himself, he probably captured him easily with the assistance of the miners which he readily obtained without doubt.

Deputy Sheriff Charles Crawford, who left here in pursuit of the murderer Hoppe, at 5 o'clock p. m. Thursday, returned Monday afternoon at 2:45 p. m., having traveled by team and horseback three hundred and fifty miles—almost an average of one hundred miles a day. The first night he rested for a few hours at Capt. Nelse's place on the Teton. The next afternoon (Friday) he met Scott at Ft. Conrad and learned that his man had been at the Sweet Grass Hills that morning. He hitched up and reached the Sweet Grass—fifty miles distant—early Saturday morning. He ascertained that Hoppe had reached the camp on Thursday evening. The first place the murderer found was Simmons' cabin where a family lived. All were away from home except a little girl. Hoppe's appearance, with his hat off and coatless, with a bloody shirt so alarmed the girl that she shut and locked the door and kept him out. She told her people when they returned that a murderer had been there. The child insisted that the man was a murderer, and was terribly frightened. Hoppe afterwards found his way to Dutch Henry's cabin, where he got supper and breakfast next morning. He told such a plausible story about how he came there that he escaped arrest and detection.

His story was that he had been traveling with some illicit whiskey traders and they got into a quarrel and tried to kill him and he escaped after having taken a shot at one of them, which he did not think had any effect. The miner's believing his story let him go. He left early Friday morning between 6 and 7 o'clock to go to the camp of the Mounted Police, north of the British boundary line, on Milk river. A MONSTROUS CRIME. A Fiendish Deed Which Has Thrown the Residents of a County Into Excitement.
MEMPHIS, Tenn., May 29.—The entire population of Mississippi county, Arkansas, is in a frenzy of excitement over a horrible tragedy which occurred one mile from Elmot, and four from Osceola, the county-seat, Sunday morning. Officers of the steamer Rosa Lee, which arrived this afternoon, brought particulars of the affair. On Saturday night, at the house of a colored man named King, there was a dance. Jack Matthews, Tom Field and George Curtis, young white farmers, went to King's house. About 1 o'clock, by their own admission, they went to the cottage of Mrs. Stokes Allen, a widow living near by with her two children, a boy sixteen years old and a daughter of ten. They could not get in, and left. About 3 o'clock the negro man, John King, was awakened by the little girl, who called out that her mother was dead. King's wife rushed over and found Mrs. Allen lying with her skull horribly crushed in, and the boy at her side similarly injured and dying. She at once ran for a doctor and alarmed the neighborhood. The little girl had returned to the cottage when the physician arrived, and was found, also, to have been fatally injured. Her breast was mashed in, and from her crushed skull the brain protruded. From the position in which Mrs. Stokes Allen was found it was evident that she had been ravished after death. Excitement became intense, and suspicion pointed to three white men and John King, and they were arrested. Matthews was taken before the little girl, and she stated it was he who struck her. Investigation is going on at the court-house at Osceola, and is daily attended by hundreds of people. Work in the county is practically suspended. A lynching is certain. With difficulty the conservative people have succeeded in holding such a course off till a full examination. It is thought the four will be swung off in open daylight to-morrow.

A Widow and Two Children Murdered in the Night.

Three White Men and a Negro Charged With the Crime.

One of the Children Lives to Speak—Beaten to Death and the Woman Ravished—Identity of the Villains Not Certain.
Correspondence of The Appeal.

Osceola, Ark., May 29.—What may prove to be a triple murder, as it had already prove to be a double murder, occurred four miles from this place Sunday morning. About 3 o'clock that morning Mrs. Stokes Allen, a widow, living in a cottage with her sixteen-year-old son Robert, and her ten-year-old daughter, was murdered by three white men and a negro, and subsequently ravished. The boy was killed while defending his mother, and the girl beaten so severely that she will die. Saturday night a dance was given at the house of John King, on J. P. Hale's place. The story goes that three white men named Robert Matthews, Tom Fields and George Curtis, being on a spree, went to the dance. Subsequently they went to Mrs. Allen's house, about a mile distant, and tried to get in, but failed. They then returned to King's. This is said to have been about 1 o'clock. At 8 o'clock a. m. King and his wife were awakened by a noise at the door, which having been opened, Mrs. Allen's little daughter was found, covered with blood, and crying, "Mother is dead!" Mrs. King then rushed over to the house and found Mrs. Allen lying dead in a pool of her own blood, her clothing thrown over her head. The boy Robert was unconscious at her side. Mrs. King then ran to Dr. Hale's, who alarmed the neighborhood. Meantime the girl had crawled back and had fallen on the floor. Eight hours later the boy died, having never spoken a word. The weapon used by the murderers was a heavy plank. The sheriff arrested the white men named and the negro King. When Mathews was brought before the girl she recognized him as one of the murderers. She subsequently made statements to the effect that she had risen about 1 o'clock to admit her brother, who had been away from home, and afterward had gone out into the yard, where she saw Matthews, King and another man. When she re-entered the house she forgot to lock the door, and went to sleep. She recalls nothing of what happened later. The coroner's jury has been investigating the case ever since at Osceola, and 500 people have been in attendance daily. Business has been practically suspended. The sheriff is guarding the arrested men closely, and the opinion seems to be that as soon as the crime can be definitely fixed upon the men arrested a lynching will occur. Thus far conservative counsels have prevailed. Osceola is about ninety miles from Memphis, and there is no telegraphic communication.

Chicago, Sept. 15.—A dispatch from Bismarck, Dak., says: A man named Wise was lynched for stealing horses in the Turtle Mountains on Wednesday. Wise was at one time a prominent citizen of Wyoming, and during his residence in that territory was prominently mentioned for the legislature. Private advices from the scene of the lynching are to the effect that Wise was overtaken by several settlers who had missed horses. CREW HAVE A NAMBOW ESCAPE.
CHICAGO, Sept. 15.—A dispatch from East Saginaw, Mich., says: Fire has been running in the woods of Northern Michigan two weeks, and although several towns and much valuable property have been threatened no serious losses have resulted up to this time. A disaster is reported on the Saginaw, Tuscola and Huron Railroad, resulting from forest fire. An express train, while running 20 miles an hour, ran on a place of track beneath which the ties had burned. The engine, express, and baggage cars, and two coaches left the rail, ran along the ground about two lengths of the train, and the engine then turned over in the ditch. The engineer, driver, and express messenger were thrown clear of the wreck and escaped with bruises and burns. The fire on the track immediately communicated to the coaches, and the passengers and crew barely had time to run through the train and escape by the run coaches before every particle of woodwork in train was burned.

A DAKOTA LYNCHING.
A Horse Thief Strung to a Tree in the Turtle Mountains.
BISMARCK, Dak., Sept. 15.—A man named Wise was lynched for stealing horses in the Turtle mountains on Wednesday. Wise was at one time a prominent citizen of Wyoming, and during his residence in that territory was prominently mentioned for the legislature.

Private advices from the scene of the lynching are to the effect that Wise was overtaken by several settlers who had missed horses. He was en route to Manitoba, and it is believed that many of the animals which have been missed in that vicinity of late, were taken by him across the border. He was overtaken in a ravine and at first showed fight, but was forced to throw down his rifle and surrender the horses. Then he was driven to the nearest tree and lynched.

Wise came from Pennsylvania, where it is said his family still reside.

Willingham of Albany was putting up a mill at the Blue Spring, The carpenter having the work in charge generally footd it from Albany every morning, eating his breakfast at home and taking his dinner bucket along. Cuthbert Liberal: Last Monday morning a young lady in Cuthbert received a fright which effectually stopped her growth for several years to come. When she arose from bed she went to hoist a window sash to admit fresh air. Deliberately she loosed the latch with which it was fastened down and as deliberately hoisted the sash, but she forgot to turn the button which held the sash in place when hoisted. Lying on the window sill was a monster snake, five feet in length and not less than six inches in circumference. The young lady dropped the sash, screamed a scream that was heard a half mile away, ran back half across the room, stumbled and fell over a tub of water, and fainted with dignity. A Seventeen-year-old Mulatto Tells the Story of His Horrible Crime.

Chicago, Feb. 29.—Zeph Davis, the young mulatto who murdered fifteen-year-old Maggie Gaughan Monday morning, was brought back from Forest, Ilis, where he was captured. He confessed the murder but denied having criminally assaulted the girl. He says he was alone in the store when Maggie came in Monday morning. After she had stood by the stove some time he told her to go to work. Words passed, and becoming angered, he picked up a hatchet and threw it at her.

"I was not very close to her," continued Davis, "and it hit her, cutting her forehead and hand, which she had thrown up. Then she began to strike at me, and fought me with her nails. I hit her again on the head and she then ran toward the little closet, I following. There was a pall standing in the closet and she picked it up and threw it at me. That made me madder than ever and I hit her again and again over the head with the hatchet. She then fell to the floor and

I SAW SHE WAS DEAD.

This frightened me," continued the murderer, "and I kicked her body into the farthest corner of the closet. I then went next door and got some warm water, with which I washed the blood off my hands. When I went back to the shop Douglass stark, a colored boy, came in through the back door, and I asked him to help me carry the bags of leather into the closet. He wanted to know what I was doing that for but I did not tell him. I covered her body all up with the bags, and by this time the other girls came in to work."

"What was your object in covering up the body with the sacks of leather?"

"Well, I wanted to hide it until night, then I was going to draw what money was due me and leave town. When I heard Mr. Green say that he intended to order some coal I became frightened, for I knew it would be put in the closet and the body would be found. I was afraid to leave the shop for dinner, and, when Mr. Green sent me on an errand, I thought I should get back before her body was discovered. When I came back I saw the patrol wagon and a crowd in front of the door, and I knew the body had been found. I hid until evening and then got on a freight train and rode to Forest, where they caught me." During his recital Davis preserved a stolid countenance, and not once did he express a feeling of regret. Davis claims to be but seventeen years of age, although he appears to be two or three years older.

O. Rugg, a prominent shoe dealer of Fairbury, died of nervous prostration on Wednesday.

A nine-year-old son of F. P. Losee, of Seward, broke through the ice in the Blue river and was drowned.

Murderers Haunstine and DeMerritt, and Forger Welch pass the time merrily in the Custer county jail playing high five.

After doing business in the drug line at Benkeiman for three months, Sol Cain was obliged to shut up shop on account of his debts.

A Ulysses man has built the "largest corn crib on earth." It is 400 feet long, 12 feet wide and 12 feet high, and holds 25,000 bushels.

One of the lady teachers in the public schools at Columbus is sixty years of age and has been engaged in the profession ever since she was twelve years old.

Supervisor-elect Alschmede, of Seward, is lying in a critical condition on account of injuries received by falling from a load of wood. His jaw is broken in three places.

Fifty men and thirty-five teams gathered at the farm of Polly Roten, widow of the Custer county farmer who was murdered by Haunstine, and husked 1,920 bushels of corn for her the other day.

A human fiend, in the person of a farm-hand named Wistle, has been arrested at Elwood on the charge of assaulting the thirteen-year-old daughter of Farmer Myers, from the effects of which the girl is suffering with a loathsome disease. Myers threatens to shoot Wistle at the first opportunity.

"That immaculate personification of gall, egotism and partisan bigotry sometimes charitably alluded to as our esteemed contemporary"—is the way a Furnas county editor refers to the engineer of the opposition paper, followed by three columns of explanation of the cause of the newspaper war.

Two Cedar Rapids young men, Bowers and Bradley, paid dearly for a little fun they indulged in the other evening. They started out in a hilarious condition, with a team, and ran into a horse on a bridge, fatally injuring it. They were arrested, and contributed $150 to satisfy the damage, and escaped from the law's clutches.

The Winnebago Indians are reported to have held a council at the agency recently for the purpose of voting on the proposition of selling a portion of the reservation adjoining Emerson on the south. Some of those present accused the agent of trying to cheat them out of their lands, and consider

able opposition to the agreement developed. Grey Wolf, head chief of the tribe, made a speech favoring the proposition, and was the first one to sign the agreement, being quickly followed by fifty others. It is still a matter of doubt what the outcome will be. There are nearly four hundred men in the tribe, so it will require in the neighborhood of two hundred signers to complete the arrangements of selling the lands. If they finally agree to dispose of the tract, it is very likely they will consent to sell the 30,000 acres which will be remaining unallotted, after the allotment, which is now in progress, is completed. Miss Alice C. Fletcher, the special Indian agent, who has this work in charge, will complete the allotment this month and return to Washington to make a final disposition of patents, etc.

Colo., Jail and Hanged.

GREELY, Colo., Dec. 29.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—A large body of masked men secured Sheriff Wollover last night, and failing to get the keys of the jail tore away the brick work around the door. They opened the outer door, broke the locks off, destroyed the cages, and took out W. D. French and hanged him to a tree near the jail. The corner's inquest is in progress, but no clew to the perpetrators has yet been obtained. Apparently the indignant citizens could not wait for the law to take its course, fearing that there was a possibility of his escape from the punishment of the killing of Harry Woodbury.

Just two weeks' ago the murder in question occurred at Evans, four miles below Greely, the details being of a most shocking character. W. D. French and his son, John Samples and John Hogan entered the house of Harry Woodbury by breaking in the door, and deliberately shot him, killing him instantly. French was a large cattle owner and farmer, and Woodbury had been associated with him this season in farming. A dispute arose in the division of 800 pounds of flour, which was carried into the court, and Woodbury won the case. French, with his gang of men, who are cowboys, went to Woodbury's residence and committed the cowardly deed. They found him with his wife and two children. Five or more shots were fired, only one taking effect. The villains fled, but they were pursued by Sheriff Wollover and a posse of men, who captured the entire party at French's ranch, ten miles from Evans. They are now confined in the county jail at this place.

He was occupying a room at the house of a well known business man in this city, having been charitably given shelter there until he could find work. To-day is the time fixed by the Circuit Court of Wythe county for the execution of Wayman Sutton, the convicted murderer of Peter Harvell, but he will not hang.

The jury and the courts believed he deserved to meet death on the gallows and so decreed, but it seems that he had some friends who thought differently and through their instrumentality the law has been cheated of one of its victims.

On Wednesday night Sutton was to all appearances securely locked up in the jail at Wytheville, but yesterday morning he was again breathing the pure, fresh air of liberty, and he is now probably enjoying sweet freedom in a distant and perhaps unknown clime.

The following special telegram to the Dispatch from Wytheville, received last night, gives the particulars of the manner in which the murderer was set free:

Wayman Sutton, convicted of the killing of Peter Harvell and sentenced to hang at this place to-morrow, the 30th, was taken from his cell this morning about 3 o'clock by a party of friends, and has made his escape to parts unknown.

His friends have been endeavoring for some time past to secure his pardon or reprieve at the hands of Governor Lee, and falling in this resorted to more desperate means to effect his release.

It was currently reported on the streets yesterday that this was their design, but no serious thought was entertained as to the truth of the report.

The rescuing party is estimated variously from twenty-five to one hundred, but it is probable that it did not consist of more than thirty men at the highest.

They came on the east-bound Train No. 2 from the neighborhood of Rural Retreat and got off the train at the cut a short distance above town.

THE GOVERNOR INFORMED.

The following telegram was received at the Executive Mansion about half-past 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon, while the Governor was at Corcoran Hall attending a thanksgiving banquet:

WYTHEVILLE, VA., November 29, 1888.

Governor Fitzhugh Lee:

A company of one hundred to two hundred armed men made a raid on the jail here last night, overpowering the guards, and released Sutton from custody. What should be done?

J. R. HARKRADER,

Sheriff of Wythe.

REWARD OFFERED.

The Governor answered at once, offering a reward of $1,000 for the recapture of the escaped prisoner and directing that every effort be made to ascertain and secure the parties who effected his release.

Later in the evening the following was sent:

RICHMOND, VA., November 29, 1888.

J. L. Gleaves, Commonwealth's Attorney, Wytheville, Va.:

If it is true that rumors of the release of Sutton were in circulation the day before such release was attempted there has been gross neglect of duty upon the part of officials in not making necessary preparations to prevent so great a violation of the law.

Every step must be taken to arrest and punish the tramplers upon order and law.

One thousand dollars has been offered for the recapture of Sutton.

FITZHUGH Lee, Governor.

The action of the Governor in sending the second dispatch was based upon information contained in a private telegram which he received from Wytheville to the effect that the rescuing party was one of small numbers and that proper diligence was not exercised in trying to prevent the work of the mob.

The Governor seemed worried about the occurrence and from the information before him did not believe the officers of the law had properly exerted themselves to prevent the rescue. "Why," said he, "there have been seven murders and two lynchings in Wythe county and not one of the guilty parties has been punished." This, he said, indicated a state of lawlessness which might be improved if the officers would only do their duty. His Excellency said if true, as he had been informed, that there was a report in circulation on Wednesday that steps were to be taken to liberate the prisoner, it was gross negligence on the part of the officers not to have sworn in special guards to protect the prison if the services of a military company could not be commanded.

NO CLEMENCY.

The petition presented to the Governor asking that Sutton be pardoned, his sentence commuted, or the time of execution stayed was signed almost exclusively by ministers of the Gospel and ladies, and of the letters which came to the Capitol pleading the cause of the condemned man very few were from the substantial citizens of the county. After maturely and earnestly considering the matter, and being unable to find any reason whatever for interfering with the course of the law, the Governor wrote this letter:

COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA,
GOVERNOR'S OFFICE,
RICHMOND, VA., November 24, 1888.

Rev. A. C. Gearheart, Wytheville, Va.:

My Dear Sur.—I have carefully considered the application for the pardon of Wayman Sutton, of Wythe county, Va., presented by you, as well as all similar communications addressed to me by others. I have also thoroughly examined the facts and evidence in my possession relating to his case.

My obligation to see that the laws of the Commonwealth are duly executed and the decisions of courts are respected and enforced, as well as the duty I owe to the people of the State as their Executive officer, demand that I should not interfere with the judgment of the Circuit Court of Wythe county in the case of Wayman Sutton, found guilty of the murder of Peter Harvell by the verdict of the jury.

Yours, very respectfully,

FITZHUUGH LEE.

The Deputy left Richmond on the 6:20 train last evening for Bowling Green, Caroline county, to see if he could identify the man arrested near that place as a suspicious character, and whose conduct since his arrest several days ago has been rather puzzling, as Sutton.

Several telegrams have passed between Wytheville and Bowling Green with reference to the man, and the description of him corresponds to some extent with the appearance of the escaped murderer.

Deputy Hurt telegraphed to the officers at Bowling Green that if their man had two moles on the left side of the neck just above the collar and a crooked finger on the right hand to hold him as Sutton. The response to this was that the prisoner agreed with the description. Upon receipt of this Mr. Hurt made preparations and started immediately for Bowling Green.

Gentlemen coming from Wytheville speak as though the prisoner Sutton could never have been released had the jail been properly guarded. One of them in conversation with a Dispatch reporter yesterday evening said: "Everybody up there tell me that the people all knew the evening before that the jail delivery was to be made, and they were expecting it. The lights in the hotel were extinguished, so that those persons who were awake could see the men as they marched to the prison. The Sheriff, instead of being at the jail, was at his house, about a square distant. Half a dozen guards in the building with shotguns could easily have repelled the rescuers, as the prison is not easy of access. William Mellering died suddenly near Huntington, Ind.

The canals of the state of New York will be closed at midnight, November 30.

A petition is being circulated throughout Ohio asking for the pardon of Mrs. Garrett, the Medina county murderers.

Capt. John Spence died in Accomac county, Virginia, Monday. He was born in 1776, and voted for Thomas Jefferson.

In the vicinity of Staunton, Va., snow fell Monday night to the depth of two inches, followed by sleet and a drenching rain.

Thomas J. Goodin, embezzling treasurer of Rawlins county, Kansas, has been arrested at Portland, Ore. He was short $16,000.

James Gillerain, aged forty five, committed suicide by drowning at Blackstone, Mass., while temporarily deranged by pain in a wounded leg.

The Umbria broke the record on her last trip out from New York, making the passage to Queenstown in six days two hours and twenty-two minutes.

The Pittsburg coal operators have resolved to cease mining after December 1, owing to the depressed condition of the Cincinnati and southern markets.

William Leighton, who stole a team, shot and killed John Shine, a pursuer, at the lumber camp of Rowe & McKeon, sixty miles from Sault Ste. Marie, Mich.

While S. C. Whitford, aged seventy-five years, who lived near Demossville, Ky., was walking on the track, he was struck by a Kentucky Central freight train and instantly killed.

Oscar Carmichael, a convict, killed Guard Gresham with a stone at the camp near Sunnyside, Ga., and, with other convicts escaped. The pursuing posse riddled him with bullets.

The senate special committee, appointed under the Vest resolution of May 14 to investigate questions pertaining to meat and cattle transportation, held its first session in St. Louis Tuesday.

Smith Book, a laborer, while walking along the track of the Pittsburg, Youngstown & Ashtabula railroad at Youngstown, O., was struck by a passenger train and soon afterward died in the hospital.

Wilson Arnold, colored, was taken from jail at Yazoo City, Miss., by a party of men bent on revenge for the killing of Capt. Robert Johnson, a white man. The lynchers have not since been heard from.

The young girl found murdered on a Chicago boulevard has been identified as Eva Mitchell, aged nineteen, lately from Washington, Iowa. She was a domestic. Several arrests have been made on suspicion.

A white man named Nolan and a negro named Cicero Bowen became involved in a quarrel at Henderson, Tex. Bowen will probably die. Later Amos Graham, colored, cut the throat of an unknown negro.

John Pfilom became jealous of Mrs. Kate Malesch at a dance at Freewort, near St. Cloud, Minn., because she danced with other guests, and on the way home shot her dead. Both are Slavonians. Pfilom escaped.

Hon. Solomon Scheu, a wealthy Buffalo malster, and prominent in Democratic circles in the state, is suffering from a stroke of paralysis. If a recurrence of the attack is avoided, physicians think he will recover.

At Nassau, N. P., Pilot Evans and his boat's crew of four men were drowned off the bar on November 12 by the capsizing of their boat during a squall. They were attempting to speak the steamer Cienfuegos from New York.

A Cuban named Isidor Cejas committed suicide in his call at Nassan, N. P., by hanging himself with a strip of canvas. He was arrested on a charge of murder committed in Havana in February, 1885, and was being held for extradition.

About 1,700 bales of cotton aboard the steamer Eiphinstone, loading for Bremen, were damaged at Charleston, S. C., while a fire in the vessel's hold was being extinguished. The cargo was insured partly in the Atlantic Mutual of New York and partly abroad.

Benjamin McKinley, a married man, attempted to outrage Myrtle Hively on the farm of J. V. Porter, near Gallipolis, O. Failing in this, he cut her throat—it is thought fatally. She afterwards identified him, but he escaped, with the lynchers in hot pursuit.

A stockman, William Duceut, was brutally murdered at his home near Tushonma, Indian Territory, Friday night last, being called from the house by a party of men, who shot him in the yard, riddling his body with bullets. Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis, suspected of having led the party, were hunted down by the neighbors and killed.

Porterfield Brock, well-to-do widower living near Gilbert's Station, Albemarle county, Virginia, was to take unto himself a second and young wife, Miss Norfolk, of Albemarle. Upon returning home with his wedding suit he was shot and killed by his son, a married man, who lived with him. During the night the patricide blew his own brains out.

The National convention of the Youth's Home and Employment association met in Indianapolis Monday. The principal feature was the address by President Hoagland and the reading of encouraging autograph letters from Governors Hill, of New York; Stephenson, of Nevada; Beaver, of Pennsylvania; Green, of New Jersey; Foraker, of Ohio; Stephens, of Maine; Larrabee, of Iowa; Lee, of Virginia; Briggs, of Delaware; Lowery, of Mississippi, and Gray, of Indiana. The object of the association is furraising employment to boys, and teaching them habits of industry and the elements of an English education.
